title: Adaptive Federated Learning for Personalized Financial Forecasting in Resource-Constrained Environments
authors: Dominguez, M. R.; Santos, J.; Reyes, A.
tldr: Proposes an Adaptive Federated Learning framework for personalized financial forecasting on mobile devices, achieving 91.3% accuracy while reducing data transfer by 87% compared to centralized ML and maintaining privacy.
problem_and_motivation: Personalized financial forecasting requires user financial data, but centralized ML raises privacy concerns, data transfer costs, and latency issues. Federated learning enables on-device training, but standard FL struggles with non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) financial data across heterogeneous devices.
approach: Proposed Adaptive Federated Learning (AFL): personalized local models with adaptive aggregation weights based on user spending similarity.
Architecture: local LSTM models on each device → adaptive aggregation server → personalized model distribution.
Adaptive weighting uses cosine similarity between user spending patterns to weight contributions to the global model.
Communication-efficient: gradient compression using top-k sparsification and quantization.
Dataset: simulated transaction data from 500 users over 24 months based on Philippine spending patterns.
Baselines: centralized LSTM, standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg), and local-only models.
Metrics: forecasting accuracy (MAPE), communication cost, convergence speed, privacy preservation.
findings: num: AFL achieved 91.3% directional accuracy vs. FedAvg 87.1%, local-only 83.5%, centralized 92.8%.
num: AFL reduced data transfer by 87% compared to centralized approach.
Adaptive aggregation (cosine similarity weighting) improved accuracy by 4.2% over uniform FedAvg.
AFL converged in 35 communication rounds vs. 52 for FedAvg (33% faster convergence).
Top-k sparsification (k=10%) reduced communication without significant accuracy loss (<0.5%).
Users with volatile spending patterns benefit most from personalized local models.
Privacy evaluation: AFL prevents raw data exposure; gradient inversion attacks extract only aggregate patterns.

key_equations.equation: w_global = Σ α_i · w_local_i where α_i = sim(u_i, u_avg) / Σ sim(u_j, u_avg)
key_equations.explanation: Adaptive aggregation: global model weights weighted by user spending pattern similarity.
Top-k gradient sparsification: only k% largest gradients transmitted.

definitions.definition: ML paradigm where models are trained across decentralized devices holding local data, without exchanging raw data.
Non-independent and identically distributed data — data distributions differ across devices/users.
Weighting user model contributions by similarity of their data patterns rather than uniform averaging.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Proposes a novel FL framework specifically designed for personalized financial forecasting that addresses the privacy, communication, and non-IID challenges. The adaptive aggregation using spending pattern similarity is a novel contribution. The 87% data transfer reduction and 33% faster convergence are practically significant for mobile PFMS deployment. Establishes that users with volatile spending patterns benefit most from personalization.
directly_justifies: Federated learning preserves user financial data privacy in PFMS.
Adaptive aggregation based on user similarity outperforms uniform FedAvg.
Gradient compression (top-k sparsification) reduces communication by 87% with minimal accuracy loss.
Personalized FL models benefit users with volatile spending patterns most.
limits: Simulated dataset based on Philippine patterns, not real transaction data. [acknowledged]
No deployment on actual mobile devices evaluated. [unacknowledged]
Scalability to millions of users not tested. [unacknowledged]
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domains 10.A (privacy) and 14.A (ML approaches) were flagged as highly relevant because FL addresses privacy concerns in financial ML. Domain 6.A was flagged as medium relevance because the task is spending forecasting. Domains 1-5, 7-9, 11-13, 14.B were rejected as the paper focuses on the FL algorithm and privacy aspects, not on specific financial literacy, user profiling, or other PFMS-specific topics.

limitations: Simulated data, not real user transactions. [acknowledged]
